scene.testo: They asked him one question. When did you know the Luftwaffe was losing control of the air? He did not name a battle. He did not name a defeat at the front. He named one German city.

And that answer contradicted an official order that Hermann Göring had issued himself. It was a direct contradiction. It was given to the men who had beaten him. This is the story of that interrogation.
The date was May 10, 1945. Two days after the war in Europe ended. The place was Augsburg, in southern Germany. Reichsmarschall Hermann Göring sat in a room full of American air generals.
Göring had surrendered to the 36th Infantry Division a few days earlier. He was flown to Augsburg. He had commanded the Luftwaffe since before the war began. Now he had to explain its defeat.
Facing him was the general who ran the American air war over Germany in its final year. Carl Spaatz, commander of the United States Strategic Air Forces in Europe. He had come with a purpose.

Beside Spaatz sat Hoyt Vandenberg of the Ninth Air Force, and General Alexander Patch of the Seventh Army. Also present was Alexander de Seversky, an aircraft designer who advised the Secretary of War.

The interrogation lasted two hours. A military interpreter carried every answer into English. Göring wore a gray wool uniform, without decorations, only the insignia of a Reich Marshal. His face was flushed, his manner confident.
He began by blaming someone else. In the early years, he said, while he held supreme command of the air force, he had definite plans. Then, in 1940, Hitler began to interfere.
Spaatz let him talk. He was patient. Then he asked the question he had come to ask. When did you realize you were losing control of the air? Göring did not hesitate. He answered at once.
He said it was when American long-range fighters could escort the bombers as far as Hanover. And soon after that, he added, they reached Berlin. Hanover. A city, not a battle.

Hanover lay deep in northern Germany, far beyond the point where American escorts used to turn back. For Göring, that was the decisive moment. Not when the bombers came, but when the fighters came with them.
To understand why, go back to 1943. For most of that year, American bombers flew deep into Germany alone. Their escort fighters ran low on fuel and turned back near the border.

From there to the target, the Flying Fortresses fought on their own. German fighters were waiting for exactly that moment. Every raid beyond the border meant a running battle with no friendly fighters nearby.

In August 1943, 376 Flying Fortresses struck the ball bearing plants at Schweinfurt. Albert Speer, the German armaments minister, recorded that ball bearing production fell by 38 percent. But the bombers paid heavily for every mile.

As long as they flew alone, the Luftwaffe could inflict losses on every raid. Then the escort fighters began to reach farther. And one man in Berlin noticed. Joseph Goebbels, Hitler's propaganda minister, wrote it in his diary.

At the end of September, he wrote about a daytime raid on Emden. The Americans, he noted, had flown with fighter escort and had therefore not suffered heavy losses. Five weeks later, his tone changed.
In a single daylight raid the day before, he wrote, we lost thirty fighters. The Americans now come with fighter escort on their daytime attacks. Our fighters are no match for them.
It is deeply humiliating, he continued, to see how the enemy leads us by the nose in the air war. A propaganda minister, writing privately, admitting what the official communiqués never said.

That autumn, Göring's fighter general, Adolf Galland, reported American fighters shot down over Aachen, just inside Germany. Göring told him it was impossible. He issued an official order that they had not been there.

That scene is told in our video about Galland. Here it matters for one reason. The man who ordered the denial of those fighters in 1943 was now telling Americans those same fighters decided the air war.

The Americans hung extra fuel tanks beneath their fighters and pushed the escort farther every month. Emden. Hanover. Then a new fighter, the P-51 Mustang, which could fly from England to Berlin and back.
It carried enough fuel to fight once it arrived. In early March 1944, American fighters were flying over the capital of the Reich. It did not take long for them to reach Berlin, Göring told Spaatz.
We knew then, he said, that we had to develop jet aircraft. Jets were his hope. Spaatz asked whether the jet really had a chance to win. Göring said yes, he was still convinced of it.
If we had only had four to five more months, he said. He spoke of underground factories and a plant that could build one thousand jets a month. Vandenberg asked the obvious question.
Could you have trained enough jet pilots with your shortage of oil? Göring said yes. Underground oil plants would have supplied enough fuel. But his other answers that evening told a different story.

Spaatz asked whether the bombing had damaged pilot training. Göring said yes. The attacks on oil crippled training, he said, because the new pilots were sent up without enough instruction, and were no match for yours.

Then Edward Curtis, Spaatz's chief of staff, asked whether the Americans had chosen good targets, especially oil. Göring answered yes, excellent. As soon as we began repairing an oil plant, you bombed it again.

You bombed it again before we produced a single ton, he said. The logic was simple. Escorts protected the bombers. The bombers destroyed the fuel. Without fuel, new pilots never learned to fly well enough.

Vandenberg then asked about New Year's Day, 1945, when the Luftwaffe struck Allied airfields in one large morning attack. Why was it never repeated? Göring gave a short answer. Orders from the supreme command.

Hitler had said there was no use bombing American planes, because more would come like bees. In 1943, Hitler himself had dismissed American production figures as invented stories. The numbers proved otherwise.

Then Vandenberg asked Göring to compare the air forces he had fought. He dismissed the Russians in a single sentence. About the Americans, he was precise. They were superior in technology and in production.
The pilots, he said, were equal. English, German and American airmen fought with the same skill. The difference was what stood behind them. Later in the same session, he said it again.

Because our production was not as great as America's, he said, we could not produce everything we needed quickly. He added that the fighters over Germany were demoralizing. After escorting bombers, they dived and shot up everything.

That included jets in the act of landing. The most vulnerable moment for a jet was the approach to the runway. American fighters waited above the airfields, and the new aircraft could not be protected.

Spaatz sent the transcript to the commander of the Army Air Forces, General Henry Arnold, with a short note. I think you will find this extremely interesting. The record was kept. The answer was written down.
After the war, Arnold published his memoirs and described the interrogation in some detail. But de Seversky, who had been at the table, noticed what was missing. He wrote about it in 1950.
Arnold, he wrote, had left out one passage. The question: when did you know you had lost control of the air? And the answer: Hanover. The single most telling answer of the session was absent.

De Seversky wrote that it was unfortunate that General Arnold, though reporting this interrogation in some detail in his book, had omitted this important passage. The one answer Göring gave without hesitation.
Why did it matter? Because Hanover was not a battlefield. It was a measure of distance. It marked the point where the Luftwaffe could no longer separate the bombers from their escorts.

Once escorts reached Hanover, no German target was safe. Fighter units that had thrived on unescorted bombers now faced American fighters first. Every sortie cost experienced pilots the Luftwaffe could not replace.
And Göring's own answer carried the evidence. Fuel shortages, short training, outnumbered pilots. All of it followed from one fact. American fighters could now go wherever the bombers went.

Remember the order. In 1943, Göring had told his general that American fighters over Aachen did not exist. In 1945, he told the Americans that the same fighters, reaching Hanover, decided the air war.
One man, two statements. The first was an order meant to silence a general. The second was an admission made to the victors. Only the second matched the facts that every Luftwaffe pilot already knew.

The air war had been lost long before May 1945. By the spring of that year, Allied aircraft ranged over Germany almost freely. Cities lay in ruins. Airfields were cratered. The Luftwaffe had been broken.

Göring stood trial before the International Military Tribunal at Nuremberg. He was convicted of war crimes and crimes against humanity, and sentenced to death by hanging. He took his own life in his cell.

That happened in October 1946, the night before the executions. The man who had led the Luftwaffe ended his life by poison. The interrogation at Augsburg remained as one of the last records of his thinking.
Asked when he knew the air war was lost, Göring named the city American fighters reached with their bombers. Subscribe, and tell us in the comments whose story we should cover next.
The order about the fighters over Aachen, and Galland's four word reply, are in our video about that scene in his train. Watch it next, and compare it with what Göring told Spaatz.

descrizione:
On May 10, 1945, American air generals including Carl Spaatz interrogated Hermann Göring at Augsburg and asked when he knew the Luftwaffe was losing control of the air. He named one German city: Hanover. This documentary follows the interrogation record, the arrival of American long-range escort fighters, and what Joseph Goebbels wrote in his diary.

We trace the P-51 Mustang, the Schweinfurt raid, the fuel and pilot training crisis, and Göring's own contradiction of his order about fighters over Aachen. We also cover Alexander de Seversky's 1950 note on the passage General Arnold left out.

This video draws on Allied interrogation records, memoirs and documented history of the air war over Germany. Subscribe to WWII Testimony for more.
